tagline.text: An active volcano rising from the middle of a caldera lake, best viewed from the ridge and the lakeshore

children.text: Taal Lake is the third-largest lake in the Philippines, a huge caldera filled with water, and at its center Volcano Island is a living active volcano. Landing on the island has been banned since the 2020 eruption, but you can still see the volcano and lake up close from the Tagaytay ridge and the Talisay and Agoncillo lakeshores.
Taal Lake sits in northern Batangas, in a giant caldera
across that has filled with water. At about 234 sq km it is the third-largest lake in the Philippines after Laguna de Bay and Lake Lanao, and it is as deep as
in places while its surface lies only about
5m
above sea level. Volcano Island, floating in the middle of the lake, is Taal Volcano itself. The island covers roughly 23 sq km and its highest point is just
, a small volcano, yet it is one of the Philippines' best-known active volcanoes, with more than 30 historically recorded eruptions.
At the center of the island is a main crater about
2km

wide holding a crater lake, and inside that lake a small rock island called Vulcan Point rises. This nesting of an island in a lake on an island in a lake on Luzon often turns up in world geography trivia. In the great eruption of

, ash blocked the Pansipit River, the lake's only outlet, and the water level rose. The residents of the old Taal town on the lakeshore, near today's San Nicolas, fled and rebuilt their town at what is now
Taal Heritage Town
. The lake, once connected to the sea, gradually turned to fresh water, and some marine fish adapted to it. The tawilis, the world's only freshwater sardine, is a descendant of those fish.
The eruption on
January 12, 2020

raised the alert to Level 4, and Volcano Island has since been designated a Permanent Danger Zone (PDZ) by PHIVOLCS, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology, with landing prohibited. The old horseback trek up to the crater rim is no longer possible, and the once forested island now shows gray slopes buried in ash. The alert has stayed at Level 1 (low-level unrest) since
July 2022
, but small steam-driven explosions are frequent. On
October 8, 2026
, the plume rose
above the crater and 107 residents of Agoncillo evacuated.
So a Taal trip today is about looking, not climbing. You can look down over the whole lake from
Tagaytay

on the northern ridge, wind down to the Talisay lakeshore to face the volcano head-on, or see the rough ash-covered slopes up close from Agoncillo on the west or San Nicolas on the south. It is only about
2 hours
from Manila, so a day trip works well, and fried tawilis by the lake and a bowl of bulalo in Tagaytay round it off.

From Tagaytay on the northern rim of the caldera, the lake and Volcano Island fit in one frame. The cafe and restaurant terraces and the roadside viewpoints along the ridge road are free, and there are paid viewing areas such as People's Park in the Sky, Picnic Grove and Sky Ranch. Clouds tend to build in the afternoon, so go in the morning.

Talisay, which covers the northern half of Volcano Island, is a lakeside town that faces the volcano head-on. Coming down the winding forest road from Tagaytay, you reach a lakeshore road lined with resorts, and the sunset over the lake is beautiful. It used to be the departure point for Volcano Island boats, but landing on the island is now prohibited.

Since the island closed in 2020, Agoncillo on the western shore is considered one of the closest places to see the volcano. You can see the rough ash-covered slopes and rain-carved gullies with the naked eye, and fishermen casting nets on the lake. Because it is so close to the volcano, it is the first area evacuated in an eruption, so always check the alert level.
San Nicolas, which covers the southern half of Volcano Island, is a lakeshore town about
10km

south of the volcano, giving a view from the opposite side to Tagaytay. It stands on the site of the old Taal town, so it pairs well with Taal Heritage Town. Ashfall advisories are issued first for the southwestern lakeshore towns, so check before you leave.

The tawilis, found only in Taal Lake, is the world's only freshwater sardine. Crisp fried tawilis and tawilis sinaing, simmered in vinegar, are specialties of Batangas and Tagaytay. Its numbers have fallen sharply and it is listed as endangered by the IUCN, so it may be caught only with traditional nets and there is a closed season during spawning. Maliputo, a jack that came in from the sea and adapted to fresh water, is another specialty of the lake.

blocks.title: Fish cages and fishermen's lake scenery

children.text: Fish cages for tilapia and bamboo raft houses float across the lake, and in the early morning fishermen in small bangkas cast their nets. Little egrets hunting fish in the shallows are a common sight. The life of the lake people right below the volcano is another side of a Taal trip.

Around Volcano Island there are several small volcanic cones rising from the shore, such as Binintiang Malaki, and the island's surface clearly shows the ash layers from the 2020 eruption and gullies cut by rain. The lake and island were designated a national park in
, a Taal Volcano Protected Landscape in
, and a National Geological Monument in
. The island looks different from every viewpoint, so it is fun to compare it from several directions.

items.title: Day trip from Manila
items.subtitle: Tagaytay ridge and the Talisay lakeshore

children.text: Take a "Nasugbu via Tagaytay" bus from PITX or a terminal near LRT Buendia station. Without traffic it takes about
2 hours
Get off on the Tagaytay ridge road and see the volcano in the morning, before the clouds come in, from a roadside viewpoint or a cafe terrace.
Look down over the whole lake from People's Park in the Sky or Picnic Grove. Admission is about
Hire a tricycle and go down the winding Tagaytay–Talisay road. It costs about
one way, and you should agree on the return time in advance.
Have lunch at a Talisay lakeside restaurant, with fried tawilis or other lake fish.
Walk along the lakeshore road and photograph the volcano head-on, then go back up to Tagaytay in the late afternoon.
Have an early dinner of bulalo in Tagaytay and catch a bus back to Manila. Weekend evening traffic is heavy, so leave extra time.

items.title: 2 days, 1 night around the lake
items.subtitle: Stay in Talisay, then Agoncillo, San Nicolas and Taal town

children.text: After viewing the volcano from the Tagaytay ridge, check in to a Talisay lakeshore resort and watch the sunset over the lake.
Take an early walk along the shore to see the calm lake and the fishermen casting their nets.
Drive west along the lakeshore through Laurel to Agoncillo and see the ash-covered island up close.
View the volcano from the opposite side at the San Nicolas lakeshore to the south, then head to
Taal Heritage Town
Have lunch in Taal town, look around the basilica and the street of old houses, then take the highway back to Manila.

There is little public transport around the lake, so this plan assumes a private or hired vehicle. On days when an eruption or ashfall advisory is issued, skip the western and southern lakeshores and base the day on the Tagaytay ridge.
Take a bus marked "Nasugbu via Tagaytay" or "Tagaytay" from PITX in Parañaque, the DLTB terminal near LRT Buendia station in Pasay, and similar terminals.
The fare is about
one way depending on the terminal and operator, and the trip takes about
2 hours
, longer on weekends and at rush hour.
Buses to Lemery do not pass through Tagaytay, so be sure to check the destination.
From Tagaytay to the Talisay lakeshore, a hired tricycle costs about
one way.
Take a bus to Batangas City and get off at Tanauan. This route has frequent departures.
From the terminal near the Tanauan public market, take a jeepney to Talisay or Laurel. Check fares and the last trip on site.
There are no buses that go directly to Talisay or Laurel.
To reach Tagaytay, take the Santa Rosa exit from SLEX and go up the Santa Rosa–Tagaytay road. It is about
60km
from Manila and takes
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes
To go straight to Talisay, take the Tanauan exit of the STAR Tollway and follow the Talisay–Tanauan road.
The road down from Tagaytay to Talisay is a steep, winding forest road with unclear signs at the forks, so keep a map app on.
Tagaytay city is served by jeepneys and tricycles, and hiring a tricycle to the viewing parks costs about
Public transport between the lakeside towns is scarce, so it is easier to hire a tricycle or vehicle for half a day or a full day.
The volcano is clearest in the
December–May
dry season.
December–February
in particular brings cool, clear days on the Tagaytay ridge, with sharp outlines of the lake and island.
March–May
is hotter and often hazy, but there is little rain, so plans rarely fall apart.
In the
June–November

rainy season, clouds and rain often hide the volcano, and typhoons can block roads. In any season clouds tend to build in the afternoon, so view the volcano in the morning. Tagaytay is badly congested on weekends and holidays, so we recommend an early start on a weekday.

There are two kinds of lodging. For views and convenience, choose a hotel or guesthouse in Tagaytay on the ridge; for a quiet stay right in front of the volcano, choose a Talisay lakeshore resort. There are long-established resorts with pools and lake views, such as Club Balai Isabel in Barangay Banga, Talisay, and several small lakeside stays. When volcanic activity picks up, lakeside lodgings may close or bookings may be cancelled, so contact them before you leave.

For food, the lake's fried tawilis and tawilis sinaing, grilled or soup maliputo, and lake tilapia are typical. In Tagaytay, bulalo, a beef shank soup that suits the cool weather, is the specialty, and long-established restaurants such as Leslie's and Josephine are popular for their volcano views; Batangas-style lomi noodles and strong kapeng barako coffee are also worth trying. Tawilis is endangered, so it is best to avoid ordering it during the
March–April
spawning closed season.
Check the alert level and advisories in the PHIVOLCS 24-hour Taal Volcano bulletin the day before and on the morning of your trip. The bulletin is issued daily.
Views of the volcano are best in the morning, before the clouds rise. For photos, plan to reach the ridge before
Turn down boat touts who offer to drop you on the island. In
February 2026
, four foreign tourists who hired an unregistered bangka in Laurel and landed on the island were questioned by the Coast Guard.
When you hire a tricycle, state whether it is a round trip, how long it will wait and where it will stop, and agree the fare first.
Tagaytay is badly congested on weekends and holidays, so go on a weekday or leave at dawn.
Tagaytay on the ridge is cooler and windier than Manila, so bring a light jacket.
Do not fly drones around the volcano. PHIVOLCS advises that no aircraft be allowed to fly close to the volcano, and civil aviation authorities also restrict flights over it.
If you have weak lungs, bring an N95 mask and water in case of volcanic gas.
Volcano Island has been a Permanent Danger Zone (PDZ) since 2020 and landing is prohibited. As of
November 2026

, even at Alert Level 1, PHIVOLCS advises that entry into the island (especially the Main Crater and the Daang Kastila fissures) and staying or boating on Taal Lake not be allowed. Check the latest bulletin.
Even at Alert Level 1, steam-driven and magmatic-water explosions can happen without warning. On
October 8, 2026
, an eruption of about
5 minutes
sent the plume up to

The volcano emits hundreds of tons of sulfur dioxide daily, and volcanic smog (vog) can spread on the wind. If your eyes and throat sting or you smell it, go indoors, and be especially careful with asthma or heart conditions.

When an eruption or ashfall advisory is issued, lakeside towns such as Agoncillo, Laurel and San Nicolas are subject to evacuation. Follow the local government and police, and do not enter lakeshore roads.
If you ride an unregistered boat, you will have little protection in an accident. The Coast Guard enforces boat registration and departure permits.
The Tagaytay–Talisay road has steep descents and sharp curves, and rockfalls and slippery sections are frequent in the rainy season, so avoid driving at night.

A city on the northern caldera ridge, popular with Manila residents every weekend for its volcano-view cafes, bulalo restaurants and cool weather. It connects directly to the Talisay lakeshore by a winding road.
A park on top of Tagaytay's highest hill, where in good weather you can see Taal Lake, Volcano Island and the mountain ridges around the caldera in every direction. Admission is about

A town moved here from the lakeshore after the 1754 eruption, with Taal Basilica, one of the largest churches in the Philippines, and a street of Spanish-era old houses. It pairs well with the San Nicolas lakeshore.
A grassy-ridge mountain in Nasugbu, west of Tagaytay, offering a half-day hike with wide views of the mountain ranges. A guide is required for the hike.
